name: createClient
description:
Creates a Defjs {@link DerivableClient} from option helpers.

Options apply in order: a later option overwrites an earlier one for the same setting, and interceptors accumulate. Prefer creating the client inside the request boundary when interceptors close over auth or tenants. Balancer state (sticky endpoint, ejections, load) and the retry budget belong to the client, so a client created per request starts them fresh. Creating the client once and deriving per-call values keeps both; passing one shared balancer to `withBalancer` keeps the balancer state only. Default HTTP/SSE fetch availability is checked when an operation invokes transport.

The returned factory is a function. Calling it with {@link RequestOptions} returns a {@link Client} value for one call and performs no I/O; see {@link DerivableClient} for how request fields are captured. The factory itself is also a `Client` and carries no request options, so it can be passed to an operation directly. The base configuration is shared by every client value and is not frozen at runtime. It is fixed by convention: nothing in the library changes it, and applications should not either. Standard option helpers copy the fixed records they own when they are applied. A custom {@link ClientOption} may still retain a reference.
signatures: function createClient(...options: ClientOption[]): DerivableClient;

exampleFiles.code:
import { createClient, withEndpoint } from "@defjs/core";

const client = createClient(withEndpoint("https://api.example.com"));

returns: A callable factory that carries the resolved base configuration.

name: withEndpoint
description:
Replaces the candidate base URLs prepended to relative request paths.

The arguments are copied in order and later duplicates of the same string are
dropped. This does not validate URLs and does not change `balancer`.
A later `withEndpoint` replaces the list; it does not merge. Zero arguments
are legal and store `[]`. The default list is empty.

The selected endpoint's pathname is kept as a directory; its query and hash are discarded. For WebSocket operations, an `http:` base becomes `ws:` and `https:` becomes `wss:`.

A missing, relative, or invalid endpoint, or an illegal request path, fails with `REQ_BUILD_FAILED` during building, before any interceptor or transport runs, even when an interceptor would short-circuit. HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket share this rule. The resolved request must keep the base origin and stay under its directory; C0 control characters (including tab, CR, and LF), backslashes, `?`, `#`, and directory escapes in a path are rejected. Scheme-like and protocol-relative forms are rejected even with leading spaces; a plain inner space is allowed and sent as `%20`. An interceptor's final `req.endpoint` is checked against its final `req.baseEndpoint` with the same rule, but it may deliberately replace the base with another valid absolute URL. Deterministic URL errors are never retried.
signatures: function withEndpoint(...endpoints: string[]): ClientOption;

When an operation runs, only the interceptors of that transport run, in their registration order. Each `{ kind, fn }` record is copied when the option is applied. `fn` keeps its identity. Changing the original record later does not change clients already created.

name: withXSRF
description:
Enables XSRF cookie-to-header forwarding for browser HTTP requests.

Import this from `@defjs/core/xsrf`. Calling it checks `globalThis` immediately and
throws when `location` or `document` is missing, including in a Worker. Isomorphic
code adds this option only in the browser. It sets `config.finalizeHeaders`, which the
HTTP transport calls once per attempt. The hook receives the outgoing headers after
interceptors and before the default `Accept` is filled in, plus the resolved URL.
SSE and WebSocket requests do not get the header.
`cookieName` defaults to `XSRF-TOKEN` and `headerName` to `X-XSRF-TOKEN` when names
are omitted.

- The header is set only when all of these hold: the method is not `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, or `TRACE`; the request does not already have that header; `url.origin` equals the page origin; and `document.cookie` holds a non-empty token. A cross-origin request does not read the cookie.
- A throw while reading the cookie counts as no token. An empty token does not set the header.
- The origin check covers the URL the library builds. Fetch follows redirects itself, and after a redirect to another origin it removes only `Authorization`, so this header goes along. The target receives the token when it allows the header in its CORS preflight. To refuse that, pass {@link withHTTPHandle} a function that calls `fetch(new Request(request, { mode: "same-origin" }))` for requests to the page origin that carry the header. Do not apply that mode to a cross-origin API whose header comes from an interceptor: Fetch rejects any request to another origin in that mode. Such a request fails with `NET_UNREACHABLE` when a redirect leaves the origin and still follows a same-origin redirect. With `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, Fetch sends `Origin: null` for a same-origin POST in that mode, where the default mode sends the serialized origin, so a server that checks `Origin` can reject it. Some engines implement this differently.
- An invalid `headerName`, or a decoded cookie value that is not a valid header value (it holds CR, LF, or NUL in the middle, or a code point above U+00FF), fails that call with `EXT_HOOK_FAILED`. The `cause` is the `TypeError` the platform threw, and no request is sent. Safe methods are not affected.
- A token from another source is set with an interceptor.
signatures: function withXSRF(options?: XSRFOptions): ClientOption;

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Cookie name and header name.

name: withSSEOnInvalidEvent
description:
Observes SSE events that have no matching event struct or fail validation.

The handler may be async and is awaited. The callback receives:

```ts
{
  reason: 'missing-struct' | 'validation-failed'
  message: { id: string; event: string; data: string }
  cause?: unknown
  signal: AbortSignal
}
```

- The invalid event is **always dropped**; it is never delivered to the stream. The callback only observes it.
- The return value is ignored. An error thrown by the callback is swallowed and does not close the stream, unless `signal` has already aborted.
- `cause` is set for `validation-failed`. Without a handler the invalid event is dropped silently.

name: withWebSocketBeforeConnect
description:
Runs a hook before the initial WebSocket connect and before every reconnect.

The hook type is:

```ts
(context: { attempt: number; signal: AbortSignal }) => void | Promise<void>
```

- `attempt` is `0` for the first connect and grows by one for each reconnect.
- Pass `signal` into token refreshes and other async work so cancelling the session stops them.
- If the hook throws, the attempt fails with an `EXT_HOOK_FAILED` fault.
- A `beforeConnect` in the request options replaces this one for that call.

description:
Sets the WebSocket subprotocols offered during the handshake.

They are passed as the second argument to the `WebSocket` constructor only when the list is not empty, so the platform can run the RFC 6455 subprotocol negotiation. They matter only when the server requires a specific subprotocol, for example `['json']` or `['v1']`.

Precedence, highest first: the `protocols` request option, this client option, then `protocols` on the endpoint definition. The array is copied when this option is applied, so a later edit of the original array does not retarget the client. Applying the same option to another client copies the array again.

name: withWebSocketHeartbeat
description:
Enables WebSocket heartbeat messages with optional acknowledgement detection.

Passing `undefined` clears an earlier setting. Defjs defines no heartbeat format: `message` and `isAck` are yours. The option type is {@link WebSocketHeartbeatConfig}:

```ts
{
  intervalMs: number
  message: () => unknown
  isAck?: (message: unknown) => boolean
  timeoutMs?: number // only together with isAck
}
```

- Every `intervalMs`, `message()` is called and its result is sent through the endpoint's `outgoing` struct as JSON text. No message is sent when it returns `undefined`.
- With `timeoutMs`, an acknowledgement is expected after each heartbeat; the type requires `isAck` then. `isAck` receives the decoded incoming message; when it returns `true`, the timer is cleared and that message is **not** delivered to `receive`.
- If no acknowledgement arrives within `timeoutMs`, the connection counts as failed: it is closed and the attempt enters the `withRetry` flow as a close that `session.close()` did not request. Without a retry policy the session ends with an `error` whose `cause` is the heartbeat timeout. A missing acknowledgement is reported to the balancer as `NET_UNREACHABLE`. A heartbeat that cannot be sent because `message()` throws or the value is not JSON is a local failure: it ends the session, is not retried, and is not attributed to the endpoint.
- A `heartbeat` in the request options replaces this one for that call.
- `intervalMs`, `isAck`, `message`, and `timeoutMs` are copied when this option is applied. `message` and `isAck` keep their identity. A getter runs at that moment and its exception escapes `createClient`.

parameters.description: Heartbeat interval, payload, timeout, and ACK predicate.

A client value carries the base configuration and one call's request options. Operations accept it. It is not callable; create one by calling the factory returned by `createClient`. Calling a client value throws a `TypeError` at runtime and fails to compile.

Flat per-call options. Each protocol reads the fields it understands and ignores the rest.

Missing nested blocks stay missing. `signal`, `beforeConnect`, and callbacks keep their identity. There is no `timeout` or `abort` field. name: WebSocketHandle
description:
Minimal WebSocket instance surface used by the client transport.

It is the DOM `WebSocket` without its event-handler properties, `binaryType`, `dispatchEvent`, and the state constants. A custom implementation therefore needs `url`, `protocol`, `extensions`, `bufferedAmount`, `send`, `close`, `addEventListener`, `removeEventListener`, and a numeric `readyState`.

The transport sets `binaryType = 'arraybuffer'` when the property exists and ignores its absence. If the setter throws, it requests best-effort closure of the constructed handle before failing that attempt with `NET_UNREACHABLE`; the socket is not left outside cleanup. When the transport stops listening to a handle's `error` event, it leaves a no-op `error` listener that it never removes, so an implementation that throws for an `error` event without listeners (an `EventEmitter`-based one such as `ws` does when it is closed while connecting) cannot crash the process after the transport has detached its own listeners. This property is an optimization, and the decoder also accepts Blob frames. This is the instance type produced by a {@link WebSocketHandleConstructor}.

  | "binaryType"
  | "CLOSED"
  | "CLOSING"
  | "CONNECTING"
  | "dispatchEvent"
  | "onclose"
  | "onerror"
  | "onmessage"
  | "onopen"
  | "OPEN"
  | "readyState"

It is called as `new WebSocketImpl(url)`, or `new WebSocketImpl(url, protocols)` when subprotocols are set. The default is `globalThis.WebSocket`.

name: defineRequest
description:
Declares a typed HTTP request endpoint.

Pass method, path, an optional input struct, and the single `output` and
`error` structs. Call the returned operation with a client and, when declared, the input.

The contract is `method`, `path`, an optional `input` struct, optional
`output` and `error` structs, and an optional `operation`. A declared `input`
always requires an explicit `builder`. `input` only defines the parameters;
the builder alone decides where each value goes. Only definitions without
`input` may omit `builder`. `ResponseDeclaration` and `BuilderField` are
internal helper types: `output` and `error` are required only when the
matching type parameter is a struct, and `builder` is
`(input: BuilderInput<TInput>) => HttpRequestShape` when `input` is declared.

`output` is one struct for the 2xx body; `error` is one struct for every
non-2xx body. Neither is keyed by status. A declaration is an assertion:
omitting one means that body is never read.

Known fields are copied when the definition is created. `builder`, `input`, `output`, and `error` keep their identity. A getter on one of those fields runs during `defineRequest` and its exception escapes the call. Other properties on the definition object are not read.
returns:
An operation `(client, ...input) => Promise<error-first tuple>`.

The checked example file passes the whole input object as `path`. This snippet maps individual fields into `path` and `query` instead:

tags.name: example
tags.text:
```ts
const getOrder = defineRequest({
  method: 'GET',
  path: '/orders/:id',
```

read. `ResponseDeclaration` is an internal helper type: `output` and `error`
are required only when the matching type parameter is a struct. The struct
kind selects how a declared body is read. Pass to `defineRequest` to get a
typed endpoint.

description:
Parsed endpoint input that a request builder receives.

Object nodes are intersected with the internal `Typed` brand, so they carry the struct that
produced them and alias, `Date`, and `bigint` encoding follow the value into
the request. Record entries and tuple items are branded the same way. At
runtime a record container is also tagged when the parsed value is an object,
whether or not it was merged. Array and tuple containers are not. `null` and
`undefined` are never tagged. Nullish modifiers recover the struct they
wrapped. Union options are distributed; intersection options are combined.
Any other struct falls back to `Infer<S>`.

`CarriedStruct`, `NullishBuilderInput`, `IntersectBuilderInputs`, and `Typed`
are internal helper types.

  S extends CarriedStruct<infer Inner>
    ? NullishBuilderInput<S, Inner>
    : S extends UnionStruct<infer Options>
      ? BuilderInput<Options[number]>
      : S extends DiscriminatedUnionStruct<infer Options>
        ? BuilderInput<Options[number]>
        : S extends IntersectionStruct<infer Options>
          ? IntersectBuilderInputs<Options>
          : S extends RecordStruct<infer Value>
            ? { [key: string]: BuilderInput<Value> }
            : S extends TupleStruct<infer Items>
              ? {
                  [K in keyof Items]: Items[K] extends StructLike<
                    unknown,
                    unknown,
                    boolean
                  >
                    ? BuilderInput<Items[K]>
                    : Items[K];
                }
              : S extends ArrayStruct<infer Item>
                ? BuilderInput<Item>[]
                : S extends ObjectStruct<infer Shape>
                  ? { [K in keyof Shape]: BuilderInput<Shape[K]> } & Typed
                  : Infer<S>;

  S extends CarriedStruct<infer Inner>
    ? NullishBuilderInput<S, Inner>
    : S extends UnionStruct<infer Options>

      : S extends DiscriminatedUnionStruct<infer Options>
        ? BuilderInput<Options[number]>
        : S extends IntersectionStruct<infer Options>

`P` is the endpoint path and `M` its method. `GET` and `HEAD` cannot return a
body. `BodyValue` is a wire value Fetch sends as is (`string`, `Blob`,
`ArrayBuffer`, a typed array or `DataView`, `FormData`, `URLSearchParams`,

`Date`, `null`, an array, or an object type with string keys); an `interface`

A header value may be a scalar or an array of scalars, and `HeadersInit` is
accepted. `query` may nest, and a nested object needs `withQuerySerializer`
at runtime. `FlatRecord`, `QueryRecord`, `PathValue`, and `BodyValue` are
internal helper types.

name: HttpRequest
description:
Normalized outgoing HTTP request seen by transports, handlers, interceptors, and `fetchHandler` after the builder runs.

`body` is already the wire value. For JSON that is a **JSON text string**;
sign HMAC or digests against that string (or other final bytes), not the
original struct input.

- `bodyContentType` holds the inferred type of the builder's body. `null` suppresses that header. FormData owns its multipart boundary. HTTP inference follows a direct write to `body` and is not copied by object spread; an explicit `bodyContentType` assignment is copied. A replacement body is detected again, so declare its type with a `content-type` header. For the unchanged body, `null` suppresses library inference when there is no explicit header, but native Fetch may add its own string type.
- HTTP never writes inferred Content-Type into `headers`; interceptors see only declared headers. An explicit `content-type` header always wins over `bodyContentType` and detection, whether set by the builder, client defaults, an interceptor, or a raw `fetchHandler` request. `body: undefined` has no library-inferred Content-Type. Signers should read `headers.get('content-type') ?? request.bodyContentType`; do not configure internal fields.
- `endpoint` is the path with path parameters filled in; `baseEndpoint` is the endpoint selected for this call.
- Interceptors see `queryParams` as `new URLSearchParams(queryString)`. A builder that returns `URLSearchParams` passes that instance through.
- `operation` is a static, low-cardinality endpoint identity for telemetry and diagnostics.
- `downloadProgress` and `uploadProgress` are the `onDownloadProgress` and `onUploadProgress` hooks of `HttpExecuteOptions`.
- `responseType` and `errorResponseType` are readonly: they are derived from the endpoint's `output` and `error` struct kinds and must not be changed. Each is set only when its struct is declared. An interceptor that short-circuits with `makeResponse` reads them to match the transport.

was present; a JSON `null` stays `null`. For a JSON representation, a string

name: HttpProgressEvent
description:
Progress snapshot passed to upload and download callbacks.

Mirrors the `ProgressEvent` fields `loaded`, `total`, and `lengthComputable`.
`loaded` counts bytes read from the upload or download stream, not bytes
acknowledged by the server. Download bytes may already be decompressed.
Unknown lengths use `total: 0` and `lengthComputable: false`. A download total
is computable only with a positive `Content-Length` and an absent or
`identity` `Content-Encoding`; compressed downloads, other encoded responses,
and bytes exceeding `Content-Length` have an unknown decoded length. A
streamed upload also has an unknown total unless a valid explicit
`Content-Length` supplies it.

name: HttpProgressFn
description:
Callback invoked as request bytes are uploaded or response bytes are downloaded.

Passed as `onDownloadProgress` or `onUploadProgress` in `HttpExecuteOptions`.
Callbacks may be async and are awaited before the next chunk is processed. A
callback that throws or rejects fails the call with `EXT_OBSERVER_FAILED`,
with the thrown value as `cause`, for downloads and uploads alike. Caller
cancellation still takes precedence and reports `NET_ABORTED`, or `NET_TIMEOUT`
when the abort reason is a timeout.

`onUploadProgress` reports progress only when the request body is a
`ReadableStream` that the caller passes. Any other body (`Blob`, `File`,
`ArrayBuffer`, `FormData`, a string, or `URLSearchParams`) is sent as built and
`onUploadProgress` is not called, on every runtime. The library never converts
a body into a stream. Download progress is unaffected.

A `ReadableStream` request body follows the Fetch rules for streaming request
bodies, with or without `onUploadProgress`:

- Chromium and WebKit accept a streaming request body only over HTTP/2 or
  later, so the call fails with `NET_UNREACHABLE` on HTTP/1.1, with a
  runtime-specific `TypeError` as `cause`. WebKit was checked manually at 27.2
  only; this repository does not test it. Node.js and Bun accept HTTP/1.1,
  which departs from the Fetch standard.
- Firefox cannot stream request bodies, so the call fails with
  `ENV_UNSUPPORTED`.
- In browsers, a cross-origin request needs a CORS preflight, unless the
  browser holds a cached preflight result, and fails unless the server
  answers `OPTIONS`. A same-origin request is not preflighted.
- A 301, 302, 307, or 308 redirect fails after the body was sent once. A 303
  redirect becomes a GET and succeeds.

`fetch` gives the same network error for each of these as for an unreachable
endpoint, and for a source `ReadableStream` that throws while `fetch` reads
it, so the error does not reliably show the endpoint is down. The load
balancer therefore receives `{ attempted: false }` for it, as it does for a
throwing progress callback (`EXT_OBSERVER_FAILED`). A healthy endpoint is not
ejected for these failures, but a down endpoint is not detected by streamed
uploads alone, and a rejected streamed upload is never retried: a
`ReadableStream` body ends the retry flow before `shouldRetry` is asked.

A streamed body has no known length, so the reported `total` is `0` and
`lengthComputable` is `false` unless the request carries a valid
`Content-Length` header. That header only sets the reported total, since
browsers do not send it. Non-identity encoded downloads also report
`total: 0` and `lengthComputable: false`, since `loaded` counts decoded
stream bytes. Cancellation releases the wrapped upload stream.
signatures: type HttpProgressFn = (event: HttpProgressEvent) => Promise<void> | void;

overloads.signature: type HttpProgressFn = (event: HttpProgressEvent) => Promise<void> | void;

name: MakeResponseOptions
description:
Fields accepted by `makeResponse` when building a synthetic `HttpResponse`, for example in interceptors.

`status` defaults to `0` and `statusText` to `''`. `url` and `headers` default
to values taken from `request`: its resolved URL (base endpoint, path and
query) and a copy of its headers. A request without `baseEndpoint` gives its
`endpoint` as written. Without a request, `url` is `''` and `headers` is
empty. An omitted `body` stays `undefined`; only an explicit `null` is a JSON
`null`.

name: struct
description:
Facade object for building protocol-boundary structs and parsing values with its constructors and `struct.parse`.

Prefer this object over importing the constructor functions one by one. Compose shapes with
`struct.object`, then parse with `struct.parse` or let HTTP/SSE/WebSocket
endpoints apply the same contracts at the wire boundary. `struct` is a plain object of helpers.

```ts
import { struct } from "@defjs/core";

const Order = struct.object({
  id: struct.number(),
  customerName: struct.string().alias("customer_name"),
});

function readOrder() {
  const [error, order] = struct.parse(Order, { id: 1, customerName: "Ada" });
  if (error) {
    console.error(error.message);
    return;
  }
  console.log(order.customerName);
}

readOrder();
```

### Primitives and containers

| Helper                                                                           | Role                                                      |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| {@link struct.string}()                                     | Text                                                      |
| {@link struct.number}()                                     | Number, `NaN` rejected                                    |
| {@link struct.boolean}()                                   | Boolean                                                   |
| {@link struct.bigint}()                                     | `bigint`, or a string that parses as one                  |
| {@link struct.date}()                                         | `Date`, from a `Date`, timestamp, or string               |
| {@link struct.literal}(value)                              | Exact literal                                             |
| {@link struct.null}()                                         | Only `null`                                               |
| {@link struct.any}() / unknown() ({@link struct.unknown}) | Any value except `null` and `undefined`                   |
| {@link struct.array}(item)                                   | Array of one item struct                                  |
| {@link struct.tuple}(items)                                  | Fixed-length array; `items` is one array of structs       |
| {@link struct.record}(value)                                | Plain object with string keys and one value struct        |
| {@link struct.object}(shape)                                | Plain object with fixed fields; unknown keys are stripped |
| {@link struct.or}(...options)                                   | First matching option                                     |
| {@link struct.intersection}(...structs)               | Every struct must match; object results are merged        |
| {@link struct.discriminatedUnion}(tag, options) | Object option picked by the value of the `tag` field      |
| {@link struct.enum}(values)                                   | String array, or the values of a `{ Name: value }` object |

### Body codecs and binary values

| Helper                                                                                                                         | Role                                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| {@link struct.formData}(shape) / urlencoded(shape) ({@link struct.urlencoded})                     | Object struct plus a codec tag. The tag applies only when that value is the request body root               |
| {@link struct.arrayBuffer}() / blob() ({@link struct.blob}) / file() ({@link struct.file}) | Binary values. As a body root they are sent as bytes; as `output` / `error` they select that representation |
| {@link struct.string}()                                                                                   | Text. As a body root or an inbound `string` struct, the bytes stay text                                     |

### Parsing and modifiers

{@link struct.parse}(struct, value, options?) parses an unknown value and returns `[null, value]` or `[StructError, undefined]`.

Every struct has the chainable modifiers `.optional()`, `.null()` / `.nullable()`, `.nullish()`, and `.alias(name)`. See {@link StructMethods}.

tags.name: example

typeTable.name: any
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts any value except null and undefined, without validation.

The value is returned unchanged, and nothing inside it is validated or stripped.

- Chain `.null()`, `.optional()`, or `.nullish()` to accept `null` or `undefined`.

- The output type is `any`. Prefer {@link struct.unknown}() when the caller should narrow the value.

typeTable.name: array
typeTable.description:
Struct that parses an array with one item struct.

- Parses every element with `item` and outputs a new array. A non-array fails with `invalid_type` (expected `array`).

- Parsing stops at the first failing element, and `issue.path` holds its index.

- Throws `TypeError` when `item` is not a struct.

`ArrayStruct<S>` is not exported. It is a `Struct<StructInput<S>[], Infer<S>[]>`.
typeTable.type: <S extends StructLike<unknown, unknown, boolean>>(item: S) => ArrayStruct<S>

typeTable.name: arrayBuffer
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts an ArrayBuffer.

- Accepts an `ArrayBuffer` only. Typed arrays and other views fail with `invalid_type`.

- As a body root it is sent as bytes with `application/octet-stream`.

- As an `output` or `error` struct it makes the response body be read as an `ArrayBuffer`.

typeTable.name: bigint
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts a bigint or a bigint string and outputs a bigint.

- Accepts a `bigint`, or a string that `BigInt()` can parse. A `number` is rejected.

- Output is always a `bigint`; an unparsable string fails with `invalid_type`.

- When encoded for the wire, the value becomes a decimal string.

typeTable.name: blob
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts a Blob.

- Accepts a `Blob` (a `File` is a `Blob`). Anything else fails with `invalid_type`.

- As a body root it is sent as is, with the blob's own type or `application/octet-stream`.

- As an `output` or `error` struct it makes the response body be read as a `Blob`.

typeTable.name: boolean
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts boolean values.

Accepts `true` and `false` only. Other values, including `'true'` and `1`, fail with `invalid_type`.

typeTable.name: date
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts a Date, timestamp, or date string and outputs a Date.

- Accepts a `Date`, a millisecond timestamp, or a string. A valid `Date` is returned as the same object. A number or string is converted with `new Date(value)`.

- Output is a `Date`. A value that produces an invalid date fails with `invalid_type`.

- When encoded for the wire, the value becomes an ISO 8601 string (`toISOString()`).

typeTable.name: discriminatedUnion
typeTable.description:
Struct that picks one object struct by the value of a tag field.

```ts
const Event = struct.discriminatedUnion("kind", [
  struct.object({ kind: struct.literal("created"), id: struct.number() }),
  struct.object({ kind: struct.literal("deleted"), id: struct.number() }),
]);
```

- Every option must be an object struct whose `discriminator` field is a required {@link struct.literal}(). A missing field, a non-literal field, an optional field, or a duplicate tag value throws `TypeError` when the struct is created.

name: StructError
description:
Error returned by a failed struct parse, aggregating one or more {@link StructIssue}s and their formatters.

`name` is `'StructError'`. Construct it with `constructor(issues: StructIssue[])`. `issues` is the `readonly` list of those issues. `message` is the issue's message for a single issue, `N struct issues: <first message>` for several, and `Struct parse failed` for none.

Default issue messages name the received kind and omit the value, so `message` and `prettify()` can be logged. For example, `Expected number at id, received string`. `message` and the formatters use that text. The raw value stays on `StructIssue.received`; custom `errorMap` text is used verbatim and can reintroduce sensitive values.

Use `format()`, `flatten()`, or `prettify()` to present issues to callers.

- `struct.parse` stops at the first failure, so `issues` holds one {@link StructIssue} there.

- `format()` returns a {@link FormattedStructError} tree. Each node has an `_errors` array, and nested keys follow `issue.path`.

- `flatten()` returns a {@link FlattenedStructError}: messages with an empty path go to `formErrors`, the others are grouped by the first path segment in `fieldErrors`.

- `prettify()` returns one `× path: message` line per issue. An empty path is shown as `<root>`.

name: StructIssue
description:
A single validation failure produced while parsing a struct.

- `code` is the machine-readable category. The parser produces `invalid_type`, `invalid_literal`, `invalid_enum`, `invalid_union`, `invalid_intersection`, and `missing_key`; `custom` is part of the type, but the built-in structs never produce it.

- `expected` describes the expected type or value.

- `message` is the final text, after an optional {@link ErrorMap} rewrite.

- `path` runs from the parse root to the failing location: field names and array indices. It is empty for a root-level failure.

- `received` is the value that failed at `path`.

name: FaultCode
description:
Every failure Defjs reports, as one closed set of codes.

The prefix before the first `_` is the class; there is no separate `kind` field.
Read the prefix for coarse triage and the whole code for an exact case:

| Class  | Meaning                                                        |
| ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `HTTP` | The peer answered with a non-2xx status.                        |
| `REQ`  | The request never left: input, request options, or build.       |
| `NET`  | No usable response: cancel, timeout, connect, truncated body.   |
| `RES`  | A response arrived but could not be read as declared.           |
| `EXT`  | Code you attached to the pipeline threw.                        |
| `CAP`  | A declared buffer limit was exceeded.                           |
| `ENV`  | The host runtime lacks a required capability.                   |

The set is closed on purpose: it keeps `switch (fault.code)` exhaustive. Extensions
report their own detail through `cause`, not through a new code.

name: Fault
description:
Union of every failure an operation can return, discriminated by `code`.

`Fault<TErr>` is {@link FaultOf} applied to the decoded body type, so it is the
union of {@link DecodeFault}, {@link HttpStatusFault}<TErr>, and
{@link PreflightFault}. `ErrorBody<TErr>` is `undefined` when `TErr` is
`undefined`, and `Infer<TErr>` otherwise. Switch on `fault.code`.

Every variant is a native `Error` named `DefjsFault`, so `String(fault)` produces
`DefjsFault: <message>`. `code` and the variant metadata — `status`, `response`,
`data` — are enumerable own properties. The native `cause` chain is non-enumerable.

Default Struct messages say `received <kind>`, never the received value. A JSON
`SyntaxError` behind `RES_DECODE_FAILED` gives the message
`Response body could not be decoded`. Structural paths retain record keys, which
may be sensitive. Raw `StructIssue.received` and parser causes remain sensitive;
custom `errorMap` and extension messages are used verbatim and need review before
logging.

Call `format()`, `flatten()`, or `prettify()` only after narrowing `fault.cause`
to `StructError`; those helpers are not copied onto the fault.

`FaultOf<Infer<typeof errorStruct>>`, or use `Fault<typeof errorStruct>`.

name: HttpStatusFault
description:
Fault for a non-2xx response, typed by the declared `error` struct.

`TErr` is the endpoint's declared `error` struct, or `undefined` when it
declares none. Any non-2xx status. When the endpoint declared `error` and the
body decoded, `data` is that body and `response` carries it. Omitting `error`
skips decoding, which leaves `data` as `undefined` and `response` without a
`body` field. `ErrorBody<TErr>` is that decoded body: `undefined` when no
error struct was declared, otherwise `Infer<TErr>`. {@link HttpStatusFaultOf}
is the member shape.

name: HttpStatusFaultOf
description:
Non-2xx fault expressed by its decoded body type instead of the struct that produced it.

Factories work in decoded values, so they use this form; endpoint types use
`HttpStatusFault` and let `Infer` bridge the two. When `TData` is `undefined`,
the body was never read and `response` is metadata alone.

name: DecodeFault
description:
A response arrived but could not be read as declared.

`code` is one of `RES_DECODE_FAILED`, `RES_MEDIA_TYPE_INVALID`, or
`RES_STRUCT_MISMATCH`. `response` is metadata only: a body is a decoded value,
and decoding is what failed, so there is no `body` field to reach for. The
offending detail lives on `cause` (a `StructError` for a struct mismatch, the
parser failure for an unreadable representation).

name: PreflightFault
description:
A failure that may have happened before any response existed.

Covers `REQ_*`, `NET_*`, `EXT_*`, `CAP_*`, and `ENV_UNSUPPORTED`. `response`
is `undefined` until the transport has metadata to report, such as a
body that truncated mid-download.

name: AnyFault
description:
Any fault at all, whatever its decoded error-body type.

Use it for handlers that classify faults without caring which endpoint produced
them. Prefer `Fault<typeof yourErrorStruct>` where the body type matters.

name: ERR_ABORTED
description:
Shared Error sentinel that marks a request as aborted.

Its `message` is `Request was aborted`. Shared `cause` and message value for caller cancellation. `createNetworkFault`
maps it, and a `DOMException` named `AbortError`, to `NET_ABORTED`. An HTTP
interceptor that throws it makes the call resolve with a `NET_ABORTED` fault.

The sentinel carries a non-enumerable `Symbol.for('defjs.cause.aborted')`
brand. {@link isAbortCause} recognizes this sentinel from any Core copy
without comparing object identity. Classification is independent of unrelated
earlier executions.

description:

HTTP interceptor function: may inspect or modify the request, then call `next`.

Call `next(req)` or short-circuit with `makeResponse`. Wrap it with
`createHttpInterceptor` to register it.

name: HttpInterceptor
description:
Tagged HTTP interceptor accepted by client interceptor options.

Created by `createHttpInterceptor`. `kind` is the discriminant that lets
`withInterceptors` accept HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket interceptors in one list.

name: HttpInterceptorNext
description:
Continuation that runs the rest of the HTTP interceptor chain, or the handler.

`next(req)` only goes inward: the interceptors registered after this one, then
the Fetch handler. It is not a new operation call from outside the chain.
Call `next` again for a safe
replay (for example one 401 refresh) from the same interceptor; outer layers
do not run a second time. Once the chain has settled, calling `next` rejects
with `HTTP interceptor next() cannot be called after the chain has settled`.

name: SSEInterceptor
description:
Tagged SSE interceptor for client option lists, accepted by `withInterceptors`.

Created by `createSSEInterceptor`. The `kind` tag lets `withInterceptors`
accept HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket interceptors in one list; only `kind: 'sse'`
interceptors run for SSE operations.

name: SSEInterceptorFn
description:
SSE interceptor function: may inspect, modify, or replace the request, then call `next`.

Call `next` (an {@link SSEHandler}) to continue the chain, or return your own
`EventStreamHandle` to short-circuit. Wrap it with `createSSEInterceptor` to
register it through `withInterceptors`.

A short-circuit handle must provide
`[Symbol.asyncDispose](): PromiseLike<void>` and connect it to the same close
lifecycle.

name: SSEHandler
description:
Terminal `next` function an SSE interceptor receives; it opens an event stream for the request.

`next(req)` goes inward only: through the interceptors registered after this
one, then the transport that opens the stream. Calling it after the chain has
settled rejects.

`EventStreamHandle` extends `AsyncDisposable`. A short-circuit implementation
that builds its own handle must provide
`[Symbol.asyncDispose](): PromiseLike<void>` and connect it to the same close
lifecycle.

name: WebSocketInterceptor
description:
Tagged WebSocket interceptor for client option lists, accepted by `withInterceptors`.

Created by `createWebSocketInterceptor`. The `kind` tag lets
`withInterceptors` accept HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket interceptors in one list;
only `kind: 'web-socket'` interceptors run for WebSocket operations.

name: WebSocketInterceptorFn
description:
WebSocket interceptor function: may inspect, modify, or replace the request, then call `next`.

Call `next` (a {@link WebSocketHandler}) to continue the chain, or return your own
{@link WebSocketSessionLike} to short-circuit. Wrap it with
`createWebSocketInterceptor` to register it through `withInterceptors`.

The chain runs once per operation. Reconnects happen inside the session it
returns and do not run it again.

name: WebSocketHandler
description:
Terminal `next` function a WebSocket interceptor receives; it opens a session for the request.

`next(req)` goes inward only: through the interceptors registered after this
one, then the transport that opens the session. It resolves to a
{@link WebSocketSessionLike}. It may be called once per execute; a second
call, or a call after the chain has settled, rejects.

name: WebSocketSessionLike
description:
Minimal WebSocket session surface that interceptors see.

Structurally compatible with {@link WebSocketSession} without importing that
type, which avoids a circular dependency between interceptors and WebSocket.
Messages are typed `unknown`.

A wrapper or short-circuit session must forward the same
`[Symbol.asyncDispose]()` teardown as its `close` / `closed` lifecycle;
returning an unrelated resolved promise is not sufficient.

name: BasicAuthInterceptorOptions
description:
Options for basic-auth interceptors, including a custom credential encoder.

`encode` replaces only the credential encoder. The default is
``btoa(`${username}:${password}`)``. The interceptor always prefixes the
returned string with `Basic `, so return the credential part alone: returning
`'Basic abc'` produces the header `Basic Basic abc`.

Accepted by {@link basicAuthHttpInterceptor} and {@link basicAuthSSEInterceptor}.

name: defineEventStream
description:
Declare a typed Server-Sent Events endpoint.

Pass path and event structs. Call the returned operation
with a client and, when declared, the input.

- **definition** — `path` and an `events` map. Optional `method` (default `'GET'`), `operation`, `input`, `error`, and `maxBufferSize` (default `64 * 1024` bytes). A frame larger than `maxBufferSize` ends the stream with `CAP_BUFFER_EXCEEDED`; the library holds at most 1024 unread events, and a full queue pauses reading the response until the consumer takes an event. A declared `input` always requires an explicit `builder`. `input` only defines the parameters; the builder alone decides where each value goes. Only definitions without `input` may omit `builder`.

`EventStreamDefinitionBase`, `EventStreamErrorField`, and `BuilderField` are internal helper types: `error` is required only when `TError` is a struct, and `builder` is `(input: BuilderInput<TInput>) => EventStreamRequestShape` when `input` is declared.

Known fields are copied when the definition is created. The `events` dictionary container is copied, including own non-enumerable keys, and inherited names are left behind. Struct values keep their identity. An accessor on that dictionary still runs when a message arrives, with the original dictionary as `this`. A getter on a fixed definition field runs during `defineEventStream`.

name: EventStreamDefinition
description:
Contract that describes an SSE endpoint for defineEventStream.

The composed members are:

- `path` and `events`, plus optional `method` (default `'GET'`), `operation`, and `maxBufferSize` (default `64 * 1024` bytes). A frame larger than `maxBufferSize` ends the stream with `CAP_BUFFER_EXCEEDED`. The library holds at most 1024 events waiting for the `for await` consumer; when they are full, reading the response pauses until the consumer takes one. No event is dropped for lack of room and the stream does not fail.

- `error`, required only when `TError` is a struct. It decodes the body of a failed handshake (a non-2xx response). The kind rule is the same as for HTTP: `string` is text, `blob` and `file` are blobs, `arrayBuffer` is bytes, and everything else is JSON.

- `input` and `builder`. The request shape matches HTTP, including `body`; `GET` and `HEAD` cannot return a body. A declared `input` always requires an explicit `builder`. `input` only defines the parameters; the builder alone decides where each value goes. Only definitions without `input` may omit `builder`.

`EventStreamDefinitionBase` and `EventStreamErrorField` are internal helper types.

name: StreamAwaitResult
description:
Await-result tuple from opening an SSE stream.

- On success: `[null, stream, open]`. `open` is the returned connection's first successful handshake snapshot for native Defjs handles or wrappers forwarding the same live `open` object; custom handles or wrappers overriding `open` use their current public `open` even after reconnect, while `stream.open` stays live.

- On failure: `[fault, undefined, open]`. `open` carries the response snapshot when the failure happened after a response arrived, for example a non-2xx handshake, and is `undefined` otherwise.

- `TError` is the declared `error` struct. It types the decoded error body on the fault.

- A non-2xx handshake is an `HTTP_STATUS` fault whose `data` is the decoded `error` body. When the declared `error` body could not be decoded, startup returns the decode fault instead, as `defineRequest` does: `RES_MEDIA_TYPE_INVALID` for a JSON declaration that meets another media type, `RES_DECODE_FAILED` for an unreadable or unparsable body, `RES_STRUCT_MISMATCH` for a body that does not match the struct. Its `status` and `response` carry the handshake status as metadata and `cause` holds the reason. Interceptors, `shouldRetry` and a reconnect's `closed` still receive `HTTP_STATUS`, with the same `cause`, so a gateway `503` is retried however its body looks.

- A 2xx handshake whose media type is not `text/event-stream` is `RES_MEDIA_TYPE_INVALID`. One with that media type and no body (a `204` or `205` on Node.js and Bun) is an empty stream: the call succeeds and `closed` settles `{ kind: 'eof' }` at once.
signatures:
type StreamAwaitResult<
  TEvent,
  TError extends AnyStruct | undefined = undefined,
> =
  | [error: null, stream: EventStreamHandle<TEvent>, open: EventStreamOpenInfo]
  | [
      error: Fault<TError> | HttpStatusFaultOf<undefined>,
      stream: undefined,
      open: EventStreamOpenInfo | undefined,
    ];

overloads.signature:
type StreamAwaitResult<
  TEvent,
  TError extends AnyStruct | undefined = undefined,
> =

  | [
      error: Fault<TError> | HttpStatusFaultOf<undefined>,
      stream: undefined,
      open: EventStreamOpenInfo | undefined,
    ];

EventStreamOpenInfo
description:
Metadata available once an SSE response has opened.

`response` is the handshake response and `url` is the resolved request URL. It is the third element of a successful event-stream result and the value of `EventStreamHandle.open`.

name: EventStreamCloseInfo
description:
How an SSE stream ended: clean EOF, abort, or an error carrying its fault `code`.

The discriminant is `kind` so that `code` can mean the same thing it means on a fault.

The value of `EventStreamHandle.closed`. `eof` means the response ended normally. `aborted` means the stream was closed with `close()` or disposal, or its caller signal aborted with a non-timeout reason; `reason` and `cause` carry the value passed to `close`. `close()`, disposal and a caller signal abort all discard the events nobody has read yet, as `EventSource.close()` does, whether or not the stream had already ended (the response ended, or it failed), and the iterator ends at once. A stop after the stream ended discards the unread events and changes nothing else: `closed` keeps its value, and an iterator that rejects with the `cause` of an `error` end still rejects with it once no unread event is left. If the caller signal aborts after open and before the stream has ended with a `TimeoutError` or `ERR_TIMEOUT`, the iterator throws `ERR_TIMEOUT` and `closed` is `{ kind: 'error', code: 'NET_TIMEOUT', ... }`; a deadline that expires after the stream has ended is a stop and discards the unread events. Explicit `close(timeoutError)` still reports `aborted`. `error` carries the fault `code` (see `EventStreamFaultCode`) and the failure as `cause`. A reconnect pick that fails after open, or that gives a URL the request cannot use (invalid, or with credentials), uses `REQ_BUILD_FAILED`. A reconnect handshake that ends the stream with a non-2xx status uses `HTTP_STATUS`, and its `cause` is the `HTTP_STATUS` fault, as for a failed first handshake. `closed` resolves when the connection ends, which can be before the iterator has read every event. After an `error` end, including a timeout, the events already queued are still delivered and the iterator rejects after the last one, unless the caller stops the stream first.
signatures:
type EventStreamCloseInfo =
  | (EventStreamCloseInfoBase & { kind: "eof" })
  | (EventStreamCloseInfoBase & { kind: "aborted" })
  | (EventStreamCloseInfoBase & { code: EventStreamFaultCode; kind: "error" });

overloads.signature:

  | (EventStreamCloseInfoBase & { kind: "eof" })
  | (EventStreamCloseInfoBase & { kind: "aborted" })
  | (EventStreamCloseInfoBase & { code: EventStreamFaultCode; kind: "error" });

name: EventStructs
description:
Map from SSE event names to the structs that decode their data.

An event with no `event:` field is named `message`. An event whose name has no own entry uses the `default` struct; with neither, the event is skipped and `onInvalidEvent` is called. Declare the event name `__proto__` with a computed own key.

A `string` event struct keeps the raw `data` text. Every other kind is JSON text: `JSON.parse`, then the struct. A bare `struct.literal` therefore needs JSON text, not an unquoted token.

Retries live on the client (`withRetry`).

name: WebSocketDefinition
description:
Contract object passed to defineWebSocket.

- `incoming` is the struct every received frame is parsed with. Frames are JSON text.

- `outgoing` is the struct `session.send` validates and encodes with. Without it, `send` throws.

- `maxOutgoingQueueSize` is how many messages are kept while the session is `reconnecting`; it defaults to `0`, which disables queueing of messages sent in that state. Incoming messages are not bounded by a count: the library queues every message the platform delivers until `receive` reads it.

- `protocols` is the static default subprotocol list. `RequestOptions.protocols` and {@link withWebSocketProtocols} override it.

- `operation` is a static, low-cardinality name for telemetry.

- `input` is the struct for the operation input. A declared `input` always requires an explicit `builder`. `input` only defines the parameters; the builder alone decides where each value goes. Only definitions without `input` may omit `builder`. The builder may return `path` and `query` only; see {@link WebSocketRequestShape}.

name: WebSocketSession
description:
Typed WebSocket session: send and receive messages, observe state, and close.

- `state` is the logical {@link WebSocketState}; `connection` is the latest {@link WebSocketConnectionInfo}. `bufferedAmount` is the native unsent byte count, or `0` with no physical socket.

- `receive` yields incoming messages already parsed with the `incoming` struct. It is one-consumer: asking for a second iterator throws a `TypeError`. A frame that cannot be parsed is reported to `onRuntimeError` listeners and skipped. When the transport fails (for example a drop without a close frame), messages already received are delivered first, then `receive` rejects with `closed.cause`. Cancellation by the caller (`signal` abort), `close()` and disposal discard the messages nobody has read yet, whether or not the session had already ended; a heartbeat timeout or a transport failure ends with an error after the queued messages are delivered, and a stop after that error discards the unread messages while `receive` still rejects with `closed.cause`. A `signal` that expires with a timeout while the session is open is not a stop, but one that expires after the session ended is.

- `send(message)` validates and encodes the message with the `outgoing` struct, then sends JSON text. It sends immediately while `open`, queues while `reconnecting` when `maxOutgoingQueueSize` allows, and throws a `DOMException` named `InvalidStateError` when the session is not writable. It also throws when no `outgoing` struct is declared, the message fails the struct, or the queue is disabled or full.

- After encoding, a value JSON cannot faithfully represent throws `TypeError` before sending or entering the queue. This includes non-finite numbers, functions, symbols, `Map`, `Set`, streams, and class instances without a JSON representation, at the root or nested. The same guard protects heartbeat messages; a heartbeat serialization failure ends the session. Struct validation may reject a value first.

- `close(code?, reason?)` requests closure and stops the heartbeat. `code` must be `1000` or in `3000..4999`, and `reason` at most 123 UTF-8 bytes; invalid arguments throw before the state changes.

- `closed` resolves with the logical terminal {@link WebSocketCloseInfo}.

- `onStateChange` and `onRuntimeError` return an unsubscribe function.

Prefer `await using ownedSession = session` for owned scope cleanup. Manual `session.close()` and `await session.closed` remain available.

```ts
async function consume(
  session: WebSocketSession<unknown, never>,
): Promise<void> {
  await using ownedSession = session;
  for await (const message of ownedSession.receive) console.log(message);
}
```

The async disposer requests native close and waits for Defjs-owned teardown, but it bounds a missing close event at one second and may reject with a `DOMException` named `TimeoutError`. It cannot prove that the physical TCP connection closed.

name: WebSocketState
description:
Lifecycle state of a managed WebSocket session.

| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `idle`         | Before the first connect attempt                                       |
| `connecting`   | Preparing and opening the first connection                             |
| `open`         | The physical socket is open                                            |
| `reconnecting` | Preparing or waiting for a replacement socket after a close            |
| `closing`      | Closure was requested with `session.close()` or disposal               |
| `closed`       | Terminal: the session ended without an error or cancellation           |
| `aborted`      | Terminal: the session was cancelled through `signal`                   |
| `error`        | Terminal: the session failed, including a startup failure or `timeout` |

Observe it with `session.state` and `session.onStateChange`.

name: WebSocketConnectionInfo
description:
Connection metadata for the current WebSocket generation.

- `url` is the URL the socket reports.

- `protocol` is the negotiated subprotocol and `extensions` the negotiated extensions. Both are `undefined` when the socket reports an empty string.

- `generation` counts the physical sockets that reached `open`: `1` after the first open, one more after each reconnect. A snapshot taken before any open has `0`.

`session.connection` exposes the session's current public connection info. The `connection` in the operation result preserves the first successful snapshot only for a native Defjs session or a wrapper forwarding the same live `connection` object. Custom sessions and wrappers that transform `connection` instead return their current public `connection`. Sharing `closed` cannot bypass URL sanitization or metadata filtering, and Defjs does not reconstruct first-connection metadata from arbitrary transformations.

name: WebSocketCloseInfo
description:
Logical terminal outcome of a WebSocket session.

What `session.closed` resolves with, once the session has ended for good.

- `closed`: the session ended normally. When the peer or the server closed it, the messages already queued are still delivered through `receive` before it ends, unless the caller stops the session first. A manual `session.close()` or disposal is a stop by the caller: the messages nobody has read yet are discarded and `receive` ends at once.

- `aborted`: the session was cancelled; `cause` is the abort reason. Messages nobody has read yet are discarded.

- `error`: the session failed; `cause` is required. The error is passed to `onRuntimeError`. Runtime causes need not carry a Defjs fault code; heartbeat timeout and exhausted reconnects can retain plain errors. A connection that was open and then dropped without a close frame (`code` 1006) is an `error` on every runtime, with `cause` `Error("WebSocket connection error")`; the runtime need not fire a native `error` event for it. Messages already queued are still delivered through `receive`, unless the caller stops the session first; it rejects with `cause` after the last one.

- `code`, `reason`, and `wasClean` come from the native close event when one was observed. A manual `session.close(code, reason)` fills `code` and `reason` when the close event does not.

A stop by the caller (`session.close()`, disposal, or an abort of the caller's `signal`) discards the messages nobody has read yet, whether or not the session had already ended (the peer closed it, or it failed). A stop after the session ended discards the unread messages and changes nothing else: `closed` keeps its value, and `receive` still rejects with the `cause` of an `error` end once no unread message is left. A `signal` that expires with a `TimeoutError` while the session is still running is a timeout, not a stop: the session ends as an `error` and delivers the queued messages first. A deadline that expires after the session has ended is a stop.

name: ManualSocketCloseReason
description:
Close code and reason recorded when a session is closed with session.close.

Records the `code` and `reason` passed to `session.close(code?, reason?)`. They fill `code` and `reason` of the final `{ kind: 'closed' }` close info when the peer's close event carries none. `close` throws a `DOMException` when a provided `code` is not the integer `1000` or an integer from `3000` through `4999`, and when `reason` exceeds 123 UTF-8 bytes. Omitting `code` is allowed.

name: WebSocketHeartbeatConfig
description:
Heartbeat settings for a live WebSocket session: what to send, how often, and how to recognize the answer.

Defjs defines no heartbeat format. `message` and `isAck` are yours.

- `intervalMs` is the delay between heartbeat messages.

- `message()` builds the payload. It is sent through the `outgoing` struct as JSON text, so the endpoint needs an `outgoing` struct. Nothing is sent when it returns `undefined`.

- After struct encoding, non-JSON values fail with `TypeError` through the same serializer as `session.send`; that heartbeat failure ends the session without a retry.

- `isAck(message)` receives each decoded incoming message. When it returns `true`, the message is the acknowledgement and is not delivered to `receive`. A frame that fails the `incoming` struct never reaches it.

- `timeoutMs` is how long to wait for an acknowledgement after a heartbeat, and it needs `isAck`: the type allows `timeoutMs` only together with `isAck`. A missing acknowledgement counts as a connection failure, reported to the balancer as `NET_UNREACHABLE`. The socket is closed and the attempt enters the retry flow of `withRetry`; without a retry policy the session ends with an `error`. A throwing `message()` or a serialization failure also ends the session, but is not attributed to the endpoint and is not retried.

Set it with {@link withWebSocketHeartbeat} or the `heartbeat` request option.

name: withOpenTelemetryServer
description:
Client option that installs outbound OpenTelemetry interceptors for HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket.

Appends one interceptor per enabled transport, in the order HTTP, SSE, WebSocket. Apply it at `createClient` time. It does not initialize the OpenTelemetry SDK or acquire global tracer, meter, or logger handles: pass the ones your application owns. Each transport can be toggled or customized via `http`, `sse`, and `webSocket`.

`options` is required. It carries `tracer`, `meter`, `logger`, `propagator`, `requireParentSpan`, and the `http` / `sse` / `webSocket` transport options. Pass `{}` to install the interceptors with propagation only.

Each of `tracer`, `meter` and `logger` is optional and works without the others. Without `tracer`, the plugin creates no local spans, never calls `trace.getTracer(...)`, and skips `startSpanHook`, `requestHook` and `responseHook`. Propagation still forwards the extracted parent context.

HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket are on by default. Pass `{ enabled: false }` on a transport to skip it.

`http`, `sse`, and `webSocket` are read once, in that order, during this call. A missing block stays missing. `tracer`, `meter`, `logger`, `propagator`, and hook functions keep their identity. Replacing a block, or changing its fields, after this call does not affect the returned option.

`enabled` is read next. Only `enabled: false` disables a block, and that branch does not read its hooks or `queryPropagation`. Otherwise the copy continues with `startSpanHook`, `requestHook`, and `responseHook`; a WebSocket block then copies `queryPropagation`. Those getters run here, once. If a getter throws, the exception leaves this call immediately and later blocks are not read. It is not caught or deferred until the option is applied.

The supplied Meter's instrument creation methods are called each time the returned option is applied to a client config, not during this call. The Meter/SDK controls instrument identity and aggregation. Each duration histogram receives its own copy of the default bucket boundaries.

Pass application-owned OpenTelemetry `Tracer`, `Meter`, and/or `Logger` handles.
This package does not initialize the OpenTelemetry SDK.

- `tracer` — Optional. Without it there are no local spans and no span hooks.

- `meter` — Optional. Without it no package metrics are recorded.

- `logger` — Optional. A `Logger` from `@opentelemetry/api-logs`, not a Winston/Pino Logger. Without it no diagnostic LogRecords are emitted. Defjs never obtains a global logger or owns its provider.

- `propagator` — Defaults to W3C Trace Context + Baggage.

- `requireParentSpan` — Defaults to `false`. With a `tracer`, `true` bypasses all instrumentation, including logs, when no active parent span exists. Without a `tracer` it blocks neither metrics nor logs.

- `http`, `sse`, `webSocket` — Per-transport options. Omitting a block leaves it unset and the transport enabled. A transport is disabled only by `{ enabled: false }`. `withOpenTelemetryServer` reads each present block once and copies its fields.

name: OpenTelemetryServerTransportOptions
description:
Shared per-transport OpenTelemetry client options: whether the transport is enabled and its span hooks, generic over the response type.

`TResponse` is what `responseHook` receives: `HttpResponse<unknown>` for HTTP, `EventStreamHandle<unknown>` for SSE, `WebSocketSessionLike` for WebSocket. See {@link OpenTelemetryServerHttpOptions}, {@link OpenTelemetryServerSSEOptions} and {@link OpenTelemetryServerWebSocketOptions}.

`enabled` defaults to `true`; only `enabled: false` turns the transport off.

Span hooks run only when a `tracer` is supplied. `startSpanHook` runs synchronously before span creation for its own transport. Its attributes are applied after built-in attributes, so the application may override `url.full` or another initial value. If it throws, Defjs creates the span with built-in attributes and continues the request. `requestHook` runs after span creation and before the request is sent; `responseHook` runs after the transport result is returned. Both may return a promise, but neither is awaited: a throw or rejection never blocks or fails the operation. `responseHook` receives the original request as its third argument.

While `span.isRecording()` is true, hook failures record `defjs.otel.hook.error` and `exception` events. The `exception` event carries only `exception.type` (the class name, not a Defjs fault code), never `exception.message` or `exception.stacktrace`, because runtime error text can include the full request URL or a response body fragment; the same rule applies to the `exception` event recorded when a transport fails. For non-recording spans (ended or unsampled), failures go to the OpenTelemetry diagnostic logger through `diag.error`. Applications must configure `diag.setLogger(...)` from `@opentelemetry/api` to receive them; there is no automatic output by default. The package does not initialize the SDK, and this diagnostic is not a separate SDK `LogRecord`.

By default, `url.full` resolves only `request.endpoint` against optional `request.baseEndpoint`; an independent `request.queryString` is not appended. That boundary is not query redaction. As the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions require, credentials in the endpoint's userinfo are replaced with `REDACTED:REDACTED`, and the values of the default sensitive query keys (`sig`, `Signature`, `AWSAccessKeyId`, `X-Amz-Signature`, `X-Amz-Credential`, `X-Amz-Security-Token`, `X-Goog-Signature`) are replaced with `REDACTED`, but the package has no other built-in redactor or sensitive-key policy. A `url.full` returned by `startSpanHook` is redacted the same way, but a URL an application writes through the `Span` object in `requestHook` or `responseHook` is not intercepted, so construct and, if needed, redact it explicitly.

name: OpenTelemetryServerHttpOptions
description:
Options for the HTTP transport — the shared options with an HttpResponse in responseHook.

Set on `http` in `OpenTelemetryServerOptions`. It has no fields of its own: `enabled`, `startSpanHook`, `requestHook` and `responseHook` come from `OpenTelemetryServerTransportOptions`.

- `responseHook(span, res, req)` receives the `HttpResponse` that came back through the interceptor, before the client decodes a declared body, together with the original `HttpRequest`. Read `req.operation` for the request identity; do not rebuild it from the endpoint or a resolved URL.

- The HTTP span ends as soon as `responseHook` returns; the hook is not awaited, so only its synchronous part can still change the span. A status of 400 or above ends it `ERROR` with `error.type` set to the status string; 100–399 leaves its status unset. An asynchronous hook rejection after end is reported through `diag.error`; configure `diag.setLogger(...)` from `@opentelemetry/api` to receive it. It cannot append events to an ended span.

- A rejection through the interceptor has no response status and does not call `responseHook`. That includes a network failure, caller cancellation, an abort whose reason is `TimeoutError`, any declared-body read failure (`BodyFailure`, including text, blob, and bytes, not only JSON), a progress observer failure (`EXT_OBSERVER_FAILED`), and a request refused before it is sent (an invalid method, a URL with credentials, a header value the platform rejects, or a throwing `finalizeHeaders` hook), which carries the platform error or the hook's own error, not a library class. The span ends `ERROR` with `error.type` set to the thrown class name, such as `TypeError`, `Error` or `BodyFailure`. Caller cancellation is `Error` whatever the abort reason. There is no `timeout` option; a deadline is `signal`.

Pass `{ enabled: false }` to skip HTTP instrumentation. Span hooks run only when a `tracer` is supplied.

name: OpenTelemetryServerSSEOptions
description:
Options for the SSE transport — the shared options with the stream handle in responseHook.

Set on `sse` in `OpenTelemetryServerOptions`. It has no fields of its own: `enabled`, `startSpanHook`, `requestHook` and `responseHook` come from `OpenTelemetryServerTransportOptions`.

- `responseHook(span, stream, req)` runs once the stream has opened, before the span records `sse.connected`. `stream` is the `EventStreamHandle` the transport returned; `req` is the original `HttpRequest`.

- SSE is traced at connection level. After startup the span stays open until `stream.closed` settles, and records `sse.connected`, then one of `sse.closed` (server EOF), `sse.aborted` (`stream.close()` or a caller abort of the open stream whose reason is not `TimeoutError`; the span still ends without error), or `sse.error` (including an abort whose reason is `TimeoutError`, which ends the span `ERROR`). No per-event spans are created. The span carries `http.request.method`, which is `_OTHER` for a method outside RFC 9110, `PATCH` and `QUERY`, with the method as given in `http.request.method_original`. Reconnects happen inside the transport without rerunning interceptors, so `url.full`, `server.address` and `server.port` describe the first connection even when a reconnect picks another endpoint.

- A non-2xx handshake is observed as a connection failure: the span ends `ERROR` and, with a `logger`, one `WARN` is emitted whatever the response body.

Pass `{ enabled: false }` to skip SSE instrumentation. Span hooks run only when a `tracer` is supplied.

name: OpenTelemetryServerWebSocketOptions
description:
Options for the WebSocket transport — the shared options plus queryPropagation.

Set on `webSocket` in `OpenTelemetryServerOptions`. `enabled`, `startSpanHook`, `requestHook` and `responseHook` come from `OpenTelemetryServerTransportOptions`; `responseHook(span, session, req)` receives the opened `WebSocketSessionLike` and the original `HttpRequest`.

`queryPropagation` defaults to `false`: the WebSocket query string is left unchanged and no trace context or baggage is written into the URL. Browser WebSocket clients usually cannot set headers, so enabling it writes the propagated context to the end of the query string, replacing any parameter of the same name. Query strings can be recorded by proxies, access logs and APM tools, and baggage values can be sensitive. Turn it on only after you accept that exposure.

WebSocket is traced at connection level. The span stays open until `session.closed` settles. It records `websocket.connected`, then `websocket.closed` for a normal close or `websocket.error`. A close frame from the server counts as normal with any code, including 1011. An abrupt drop without a close frame (1006) ends the session in error and logs once, on every runtime. A caller abort of an open session is also `websocket.error`: the span ends `ERROR` and no log is emitted, except when the abort reason is `TimeoutError`, which is treated as a connection failure and logs once. `error.type` follows the abort reason: `AbortError` for a default `abort()`, the `Error.name` of an `Error` reason, `string` for a string reason. An abort while the WebSocket is still connecting ends the span `ERROR` with `error.type` `DefjsFault`. No per-message spans are created. The span carries `http.request.method` `GET`, the method of the opening handshake. `url.full` uses the `ws:` or `wss:` form of the connection URL. As with SSE, connection attributes describe the first connection; a reconnect to another endpoint does not change them.

Pass `{ enabled: false }` to skip WebSocket instrumentation. Span hooks run only when a `tracer` is supplied.

name: DerivableClient
description:
Callable root client returned by `createClient`.

A factory is a {@link Client} that carries no request options, so it can be passed to an operation directly. Calling it with {@link RequestOptions} returns a plain, non-callable `Client` value for one call and performs no I/O. That value cannot be called again: `client()()` fails to compile and throws a `TypeError` at runtime. `client()` and `client(undefined)` store no request options. `client({})` keeps the empty snapshot produced by reading each top-level field; it is not dropped by inspecting keys.

Each provided field is read once, in declaration order, onto a new options object. A `protocols` array is copied. `heartbeat` copies `intervalMs`, `isAck`, `message`, and `timeoutMs`. `retry` copies `maxRetries`, `delayMs`, `factor`, `maxDelayMs`, `jitter`, `attemptTimeoutMs`, a `methods` array, `shouldRetry`, and `budget`. Missing nested blocks stay `undefined` and do not enable heartbeat or retry. `signal`, `beforeConnect`, and every callback keep their identity. A getter on these fixed fields runs during the call. If it throws, the exception escapes and is not converted into a fault; the factory stays usable.

Endpoint selected for one call.

be attributed to the endpoint.

the runtime defines it, and that can end a Bun or Deno process that has no

name: PickFaultCode
description:
Neutral attempt outcome codes observed through `end` and `done`.

`end` reports the beginning of a peer response; later failures can still give
`done` a different `code`. Unavailability and server failures describe a peer
that answered, while unreachable and timeout outcomes describe transport failures.
Normal completion and application errors do not themselves create failure samples.

`NET_UNAVAILABLE`; other statuses at least 500 map to `NET_SERVER_ERROR`.
Incomplete HTTP bodies retain `NET_BODY_INCOMPLETE` and their status.
An SSE body-read rejection, a WebSocket heartbeat acknowledgement timeout,
or an opened WebSocket's close code 1006 or 1015 (no close frame arrived)
maps to `NET_UNREACHABLE`, without a status; a WebSocket close frame with
1012 or 1013 maps to `NET_UNAVAILABLE`, even when the engine dispatched no
`open` event before it; both unless timeout or cancellation takes priority.
Other close codes are not failures, whatever `wasClean` reports: engines
disagree on it for a server-initiated close.

name: DoneInfo
description:
Outcome of the attempt that used the selected endpoint.

`attempted: false` means no attempt is attributed to that endpoint: nothing
was sent, the attempt ended by caller cancellation or `close()`, or `fetch`
rejected a streamed HTTP request body with a network error before any
response. Both `code` and `status` are then absent. `attempted: true` with no
`code` means the peer answered without a classified failure. Built-in balancers
read only the neutral `code`, never `status`.

A streamed HTTP request body is a caller-supplied `ReadableStream`. `fetch`
rejects it with the same network error for a refused connection, an HTTP/1.1 connection, a redirect that cannot
replay the stream, a failed CORS preflight, and a source stream that throws,
so that error does not reliably show the endpoint is down and is reported as
`{ attempted: false }`. The cost is that a genuinely down endpoint is not
detected by streamed uploads alone: they do not switch `pickFirst` away from
it and do not count toward `outlierDetection`.

name: pickFirstBalancer
description:
Sticky failover balancer. The default when a client sets no balancer.

Uses the first endpoint until `done` reports
`{ attempted: true, code: "NET_UNREACHABLE" }` or `NET_UNAVAILABLE` for the
endpoint that is still sticky. The next `pick` then moves
to the following endpoint and wraps to the first. Other results, including timeouts and
`attempted: false`, keep the current endpoint. Overlapping failures advance
one step: a `done` that finds the sticky endpoint already changed does nothing.

Order and the sticky endpoint follow `members`. When the sticky endpoint is
not among this pick's `endpoints`, as when a wrapper filters candidates, the
pick takes the next candidate after it in member order without moving it, so
a narrowed pick never changes where later calls go. Only a sticky endpoint missing from `members`
resets the order to the first.

`shuffle: true` assigns each endpoint a random sort key on first sight and
sticks to that order. Keys survive a shorter endpoint list. The default is
`false`. Shuffle history keeps at least 256 endpoints, and at least the
current members, in least-recently-used order; a forgotten endpoint gets a new
random key when it returns.

`failbackMs`, when set, returns to the first endpoint by time
alone: once the sticky endpoint has been away from the first for that long, the
next pick whose candidates include the first selects it and makes it sticky
again. Nothing judges whether the first endpoint has recovered. If it fails
again, the ordinary advance rule above moves on and the time starts anew.
Choose an interval longer than the time between picks, such as a reconnect
delay, or every pick returns to the first endpoint. No background timer is
created.

Every successful `pick` returns `done`. An empty candidate list returns
`[ERR_NO_CANDIDATE, undefined]`.

Health filtering is off by default. Supply `outlierDetection: {}` to enable
default ejection, or configure its thresholds and application health function.

name: roundRobinBalancer
description:
Round-robin balancer, with nginx smooth weighting when `weights` is set.

Without `weights`, a counter starts at a random `uint32` and each `pick`
returns `endpoints[counter % length]`, then increments the counter modulo
2^32. With `weights`, each pick adds an endpoint's weight to its current
value, selects the highest value (earlier candidate on a tie), and subtracts
the total weight of this candidate list. Members left out of this pick's
candidates keep their current value, as nginx skips a peer that is down. A
missing weight is 1. Weights for endpoints not in the list are ignored.
Selection and the cleanup of current values for endpoints that left the
members take O(member count + candidate count) work per pick. Extreme weights
are scaled to avoid overflow; ratios below floating-point precision may round
to zero. Finite positive weights never produce a non-candidate selection.

Without `weights`, every pick advances the counter, including a pick made for
a retry or a stream reconnect. Without `outlierDetection`, and with calls
that run one after another, an endpoint that fails persistently therefore
receives more than 1/n of the first attempts. With exactly two endpoints and
retries enabled it receives all of them, so every call needs one retry.
Concurrent calls interleave their picks and break this pattern.

Health filtering is off by default, so successful picks omit `done`. Supply
`outlierDetection: {}` to enable it: five consecutive attributed failures then
eject an endpoint temporarily. An empty
candidate list returns `[ERR_NO_CANDIDATE, undefined]`.

returns: A new balancer. Each call has its own counter and weight state.
