name: withRetry
description:
Enables retries for HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket, with backoff and an optional policy function.

Retries are opt-in: without this option every call makes one attempt, and an HTTP call creates no retry budget. Calling it with no argument or `{}` enables the defaults: 3 retries after the first attempt, a 1000 ms delay that doubles per retry up to 30000 ms, and jitter of 0.2. The same options apply to every transport; see {@link RetryOptions} for the decision order after a failure and for what counts as a retryable failure on each one.

- HTTP retries a method in `methods` when the attempt got no response, got a 502, 503, or 504, or ran out of `attemptTimeoutMs`. Each retry rebuilds the request, reruns the complete interceptor chain, and lets the balancer pick again from every endpoint, so a single endpoint is tried again after the delay. Local failures before Fetch starts are not retried. Retry eligibility checks every method actually sent by the attempt, after interceptor rewrites; with no transport invocation it uses the defined method. A `budget` limits how many retries the client can make.
- SSE retries a method in `methods` after a handshake network failure, a 502, 503, or 504 handshake, an attempt timeout, or a network error after the stream opened. Normal EOF ends the stream. The `retry:` field of the server replaces `delayMs`, and the next attempt sends `Last-Event-ID`. A successful handshake resets the count.
- WebSocket retries every close that `session.close()` did not request, including a connection that never opened and a heartbeat timeout. A successful `open` resets the count.
- A `ReadableStream` request body, a caller abort, a manual close, and fatal errors end the call without a retry and without calling `shouldRetry`.

Callers that need a time limit without retries use `withRetry({ maxRetries: 0, attemptTimeoutMs })`. The signal of the caller covers all attempts and waits. A later `withRetry` replaces the policy as a whole, and passing `undefined` is the same as passing `{}`; pass `{ maxRetries: 0 }` to turn retries off after enabling them. The `methods` array and the `budget` record are copied when the option is applied. A request option `retry` replaces this policy for one call, except `budget`, which stays with the client.

name: RetryOptions
description:
Opt-in retry policy for HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket.

Call {@link withRetry}() or pass `{}` to enable retries with the defaults. Without a policy every call makes one attempt. Per call, `client({ retry })` replaces the client's policy as a whole value.

After each failed attempt the policy decides in this order:

1. A caller abort, a manual `close()`, a fatal error such as a mismatched media type, a WebSocket whose constructor throws, and a `ReadableStream` request body end the call. `shouldRetry` is not called.
2. When `maxRetries` retries have been made, the call ends. `shouldRetry` is not called.
3. `shouldRetry(context)` decides. Without it, `context.retryable` does.
4. HTTP only: a retry that the `budget` cannot pay for ends the call.
5. The call waits for the backoff delay, then the balancer picks an endpoint again. Every endpoint is a candidate, including the one that just failed, so a single endpoint is tried again after the delay.

typeTable.description: Retries after the first attempt. Defaults to 3; `0` never retries. For SSE and WebSocket the count restarts when a connection is established again.

typeTable.name: delayMs
typeTable.description: Initial backoff delay in milliseconds. Defaults to 1000. Zero skips waiting.

typeTable.name: factor
typeTable.description: Multiplier applied to the delay for each further retry. Defaults to 2. The first retry waits `delayMs`.

typeTable.name: maxDelayMs
typeTable.description: Cap on the final delay in milliseconds, jitter included. Defaults to 30000; `Infinity` removes the cap. The platform timer limit of `2_147_483_647` still applies.

typeTable.name: jitter
typeTable.description: Multiplicative jitter in [0, 1]. Defaults to 0.2, plus or minus twenty percent.

typeTable.name: attemptTimeoutMs
typeTable.description:
Time limit for one attempt in milliseconds. Unset by default. HTTP counts from the call to the end of the response body, SSE to the response headers, WebSocket to `open`. An attempt that runs out is a failure that the policy handles like a connection failure.
Use `withRetry({ maxRetries: 0, attemptTimeoutMs })` for a time limit without retries.

It may return a promise, which the caller's signal can cancel. A throw ends the call with `EXT_HOOK_FAILED` and the thrown value as `cause`; an open SSE stream reports that code in `closed.code`, and an open WebSocket session ends with `closed.kind: "error"` and the thrown value as `closed.cause`.

Defaults: 20% plus 10 retries/second of reserve over a 10000 ms TTL.

name: OutlierDetectionOptions
description:
Failure counting that ejects an endpoint for a while, and an optional
application-defined health check.
The library does not know what healthy means. It counts classified failures,
ejects an endpoint by time, and puts it back when the time is up; only
`isHealthy` can say that an endpoint is unfit, and only the application
supplies it. No timers, ejection quotas, settlement grid, or slow start are used.

typeTable.description: Consecutive failures that eject an endpoint; defaults to 5 (Finagle). Zero disables passive breaking.

typeTable.name: minPenaltyMs
typeTable.description: First penalty in milliseconds, also the step added per level; defaults to 1000 ms (Linkerd).

typeTable.name: maxPenaltyMs
typeTable.description: Penalty cap in milliseconds, at least `minPenaltyMs`; defaults to 60000 ms (Linkerd).

typeTable.name: jitterRatio
typeTable.description: Jitter ratio from 0 to 1; defaults to 0.5 (Linkerd).

typeTable.name: isFailure
typeTable.description:
Synchronous rule that decides which outcomes count toward ejection. The
default counts every outcome with a `code`. It is a trigger for time-based
ejection, not a judgement of health; replace it to count differently. A
throw is not caught here; it leaves `done` and is contained and reported
like any other `done` failure.

typeTable.name: isHealthy
typeTable.description:
The only health judgement. Synchronous, called on every pick for each
endpoint that is not currently ejected (an ejected endpoint is not asked),
so it should read state that the application keeps up to date. An
endpoint for which it returns `false` is not selected. Returning `true`
does not end an ejection: the endpoint must also not be ejected. A throw is
not caught here; `pickEndpoint` reports it as `REQ_BUILD_FAILED` with the
thrown value as `cause`.

name: outlierDetection
description:
Wraps a strategy with consecutive-failure ejection by time.
Five attributed failures eject an endpoint by default. The penalty is the
minimum penalty (1s by default) times the penalty level, so successive
ejections last 1s, 2s, 3s and so on; uniform positive jitter of up to 0.5
times the base is added, and the total caps at 60s. When the time is up the
endpoint is selectable again; nothing probes it or decides that it has
recovered. As in gRPC outlier detection (gRFC A50) a success never clears the
penalty level: every ejection raises it by one and every ten seconds without
one lowers it by one, evaluated when the endpoint is next used. An endpoint
that accepts a connection and then drops it is therefore ejected for longer
each time, as long as its failures return faster than one level decays.
Every classified failure code fails by default, including NET_TIMEOUT and
NET_BODY_INCOMPLETE, as Envoy's consecutive 5xx and gRPC outlier detection
count timeouts and resets; `isFailure` replaces that rule. An attempted
outcome without a code resets the streak; unattributed attempts leave it
unchanged. The outcome of an attempt that began before an
ejection, or while the endpoint was ejected, is ignored even if it arrives
after the endpoint is selectable again, so late results do not eject it anew.
The child receives the filtered candidates as `endpoints` and the unfiltered
`members`, so ejection does not look like a membership change to it.
`isHealthy`, when supplied, is the only health judgement and combines with
ejection by AND: it can keep an endpoint out, and `true` cannot let an ejected
endpoint in. If it rejects every endpoint that is not ejected, it is ignored
for that pick. If every endpoint is ejected, the original current list is
used (Finagle panic mode). Unlike Envoy and gRPC A50 there is no ejection
quota. All callbacks are synchronous; no timer is created. Configuration is
captured at construction.
History holds at least 256 endpoints, and at least the current list, shared
across endpoint lists. LRU clean or expired states are evicted first, then
partial failure sequences, then the oldest protected state only if every
retained endpoint is ejected. Temporary candidate exclusion does not itself
erase a penalty.

`defaultRttMs` defaults to 30 and `decayMs` to 10000 (Linkerd). Pending is reserved when `pick` selects the endpoint, so
concurrent picks in one tick see each other, and releases at `end`, the
beginning of a peer response (tower CompleteOnResponse), or at `done` when no
response began. RTT is the real start-to-end duration for every transport,
including failures. Higher samples replace the estimate; lower samples blend
exponentially, as in tower PeakEwma. Idle estimates decay toward zero. A done
without end creates no sample. Health filtering is off by default; with
`outlierDetection: {}` it ejects quickly failing endpoints. There is no
synthetic failure penalty.
Unlike Envoy and gRPC A48, draws are without replacement.
Load history keeps at least 256 endpoints, and at least the current members, in
LRU order, evicting idle entries first; an in-flight entry is evicted only if
all retained entries are busy. Evicted endpoints restart from the configured
initial estimate.
